title: The Tool Decathlon: Benchmarking Language Agents for Diverse, Realistic, and Long-Horizon Task Execution
one_liner: Toolathlon tests language agents on long, multi-application workflows in realistic software states so that benchmark scores reflect real tool use rather than toy tasks.
lead: Many agent benchmarks are too easy in exactly the ways that matter most. They use narrow domains, short task chains, or synthetic environments with little state complexity. That lets an agent look capable even when it cannot manage a real workflow that spans email, calendars, databases, documents, and operational tools. Toolathlon is designed to close that gap. It covers 32 applications and 604 tools, starts from realistic software states, and uses execution-based checks on 108 tasks that take about 20 tool turns on average. The paper's main result is uncomfortable but useful: even top systems still fail most of these tasks, which means the benchmark is measuring a real capability gap rather than rewarding shallow pattern matching.

problem.h2: Why current agent benchmarks understate the real difficulty
paras: A real software task often spans several systems. An agent may need to read email, check a calendar, inspect a file, query a database, and then write an output into a separate application. Each step depends on the current state of those systems. If the benchmark hides that state complexity or shortens the workflow too much, then a passing score says little about whether the agent can work in a realistic environment.

Many earlier benchmarks emphasize functional realism but not state realism. A tool may exist, but the surrounding world is too simple: too few users, too few records, too little noise, and too few cross-application dependencies. Toolathlon argues that a serious benchmark needs diversity of applications, diversity of starting states, long task horizons, and strict execution-based grading because each part blocks a different shortcut.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Build a benchmark where language agents must solve long, verifiable workflows across many real software applications and realistic starting states, so that success requires actual tool competence.

panels.title: 1. One task touches many apps
panels.caption: A realistic workflow crosses application boundaries, so one-tool benchmarks miss the hard part.

panels.title: 2. Real starting state
panels.caption: The environment contains real clutter and dependencies because easy starting states hide planning errors.

panels.title: 3. Long horizon
panels.caption: The agent must keep a plan across many steps because a short task can be solved by shallow local choices.

panels.title: 4. Strict checking
panels.caption: A task counts only if the environment ends in the required state.

panels.title: 5. Current models struggle
panels.caption: Low success rates reveal a real capability gap because the benchmark removes many easy shortcuts.

steps.b: Step 1: Provide many applications and tools
steps.text: Expose agents to 32 applications and 604 tools so that evaluation covers everyday and professional software rather than one narrow domain.
Populate the environments with real courses, sheets, reports, and records because state realism is needed for planning mistakes to surface.
Create 108 tasks that require roughly 20 interaction turns on average, so that the benchmark measures persistence and error recovery.

steps.b: Step 4: Let the agent act through tool calls
steps.text: The model must decide which application to use, what action to take, and when to switch context across systems.

steps.b: Step 5: Grade by final environment state
steps.text: Dedicated evaluation scripts inspect the resulting software state so that a task only passes if the work was actually completed.

paras: The paper changes agent evaluation from short or narrow tool tasks into a broad execution benchmark with realistic environments, long horizons, and strict verification.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: stateful workflow difficulty
hidden.name: how much real planning and memory a task requires once the software state is realistic
paras: The benchmark is really measuring stateful workflow difficulty. That quantity rises when success depends on remembering earlier findings, handling cross-application dependencies, and navigating cluttered software states. It falls when the environment is empty or the task chain is too short.

Toolathlon is valuable because it makes that hidden quantity visible. The low scores of strong models are informative because they show that current systems still struggle when realistic state, long horizon, and multi-app coordination are present at the same time.

heat.caption: Dark cells mark the hard parts of realistic tool work that disappear in simplified benchmarks.

reads.html: The hard part is not calling one tool. It is keeping track of a messy, changing software world across many connected steps.
Toolathlon increases evaluation difficulty through realistic initial states, broad tool coverage, and long-horizon tasks with execution-based verification.

paras: A benchmark only predicts real deployment quality if it contains the failure modes that appear in deployment. Toolathlon works because it includes several of those failure modes at once: wrong tool choice, forgotten intermediate facts, state misreads, cross-application mistakes, and errors that only surface many steps later.

The realistic environment state is essential because agents often fail when there is too much competing information. An empty spreadsheet or a clean inbox does not test whether the system can search, compare, and update the right record. A busy real-world state does.

Execution-based grading matters because free-form judging can miss hidden mistakes. A final environment-state check forces the benchmark to ask whether the work was actually completed. That makes low scores more trustworthy because they reflect real failures, not style preferences in evaluation.

stages.s: agent carries facts across many turns
evaluation scripts inspect the final state

math.words: Task success is the fraction of benchmark tasks whose final software state satisfies the dedicated evaluation script after the agent finishes its tool sequence.
math.equation: success_rate = (# tasks whose final state passes evaluation) / (# total tasks)
symbols: # tasks whose final state passes evaluation
the number of tasks completed correctly according to the environment-state checker
the full set of benchmark tasks being evaluated

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose an agent is tested on 108 tasks.
If it completes 32 tasks exactly, then the score is 32 / 108 = 0.296.
That is about 29.6 percent, which is close to the best reported range in the paper.
The other 76 tasks fail because at least one required environment change was missing or wrong.
This score matters because the checker looks at the final software state, not at how fluent the agent sounded.

math.note: The paper's execution-based metric matters because it ties score directly to completed work.

charts.title: Best reported closed model
charts.note: Even the top closed model solves fewer than one third of tasks because the benchmark requires sustained correct work across realistic software states.

charts.title: Best reported open-weights model
charts.note: The top open model trails further because broad real-world tool use still demands planning and state tracking that current systems do not handle reliably.

items.b: The benchmark may age as software changes.
items.html: Applications evolve over time, so maintenance is required because broken connectors or changed interfaces can invalidate tasks.

items.b: Agents may fail for avoidable interface reasons.
items.html: A model can miss a task because it misuses one tool argument even when the higher-level plan is right, so detailed traces are still needed beside the final score.

items.b: Coverage is broad but not universal.
items.html: Thirty-two applications are a strong start, but real work is larger than any fixed suite, so some deployment settings will still be missing.
The benchmark is most useful when the environments stay maintained and the evaluation scripts keep checking real end states rather than intermediate guesses.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a compact benchmark with three to five connected applications, realistic seeded states, and ten long tasks that require cross-application coordination. Include execution scripts that inspect the final environment state. Compare a short-horizon toy benchmark score with the realistic benchmark score for the same model. The demo should show a clear drop on the realistic version because long-horizon, stateful tool work is substantially harder.
demo.metric_eq: difficulty_gap = toy_success_rate - realistic_success_rate; mean_turns = total_tool_turns / total_tasks
demo.closing: The demo must make visible that realistic state and long horizon expose failures that a narrow toy benchmark hides.
